analysis.one_liner: Counts GI Bill and military tuition money against a federal funding cap on for-profit colleges.
analysis.headline: The bill died in a Senate committee without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law says for-profit colleges can get no more than 90% of their revenue from federal student aid. But money from GI Bill benefits and military tuition programs didn't count toward that cap, so a school could collect huge amounts of taxpayer-funded veteran and service-member tuition while still technically meeting the limit. This bill would count all federal education money toward the cap, and would cut a school off from all federal education programs for at least two years if it failed the limit two years running. The bill never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Service members, veterans, and their families whose education benefits would no longer be harvested by for-profit schools skirting the funding cap. Taxpayers also benefit, because federal education dollars would be capped overall rather than just the Title IV slice.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Service members and veterans using education benefits

how_it_helps.text: Counts all federal educational assistance — GI Bill chapters of title 38, Defense Department tuition programs under title 10, and Homeland Security programs — toward the 90% federal revenue limit for for-profit colleges [S3].

A for-profit school that fails the limit for two consecutive fiscal years becomes ineligible for all federal educational assistance programs for at least two years, and must meet full compliance requirements for two years to regain eligibility [S3].

The Departments of Defense and Veterans Affairs would be required to cut off aid at ineligible schools and publicly post the school's name, the extent of its violation, and how long it is barred [S3].

analysis.who_pays: For-profit colleges, which could lose access to GI Bill, Defense Department, and other federal education dollars if they rely too heavily on them — and potentially their students, if a sanctioned school closes.
analysis.who_pays_short: For-profit colleges dependent on military students

drawbacks.text: The enforcement is strict: two consecutive years of failing the limit means a school loses all federal education funding for at least two years and must prove two years of compliance to get back in, which could push some schools to close abruptly and strand enrolled students mid-program [S3].
A school losing eligibility could reduce education options in some communities, particularly online programs that service members deployed overseas use.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change is narrow and protective: it closes a known gap that let schools treat veteran benefits as private revenue. The main cost falls on schools that would fail the limit, and the strict two-year cutoff carries some risk of sudden closures that strand students. On balance the protections for service members and veterans outweigh that risk, though the enforcement design could have been gentler.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate education committee, which never acted on it, and it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Carper introduced the bill on September 17, 2014 [S1].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S5].
The committee took no further action, and the bill expired when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For-profit colleges that collect military and veteran tuition dollars kept full access to those funds, and veterans remain exposed to schools that skirt the federal revenue cap.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: For-profit colleges collecting GI Bill dollars

for.name: Thomas R. Carper
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to count military and veteran education benefits toward the federal revenue cap on for-profit colleges

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.role: Committee of referral; held no hearing or markup
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never took it up before the Congress ended

against.name: For-profit college industry
against.role: Industry dependent on federal education dollars, including veteran benefits
against.what_they_did: Opposed tightening the 90/10 rule in this period, as its members' revenues depended on military and veteran enrollment

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever held; the bill had one Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors of either party, so no partisan pattern is visible in the record.

industries.note: These schools earn tuition largely from federal education programs, including GI Bill and military tuition assistance. Counting that money toward the 90% cap and cutting off violators would directly reduce their revenue, and their interest runs against the service members and veterans the bill protects.
